To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) biofilm-grown bacterial communities express properties distinct from those of planktonic cells; (b) biofilm-growth conditions induce the expression of a stress response in some bacteria; (c) the physical and/or chemical properties of biofilm exopolysacchrides could confer resistance by exclusion; (d) biofilm-groun cells could develop a biofilm specific biocide-resistant phenotype; and (e) it is likely that multiple mechanisms are responsible for biocide resistance
biofilm-growth and the stress response are important determinants of resistance to biocides.
biofilms are resistant to antimicrobial agents and that this resistance can be due to several different mechanisms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new antimicrobial agents that target the unique properties of biofilm-grown microorganisms.
the mechanisms of antimicrobial resistance in biofilms and with the development of novel antimicrobial agents for the treatment and prevention of biofilm-associated infections.
the molecular mechanisms by which bacteria develop resistance to antibiotics, biocides and other toxic agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

biofilm-growth per se is not responsible for resistance to antimicrobial biocides, but rather that it is the result of multiple resistance mechanisms, some of which are not specific to biofilm-growth.
the biofilm phenotype is not necessarily resistant to antimicrobial agents, but that biofilm-growth can induce resistance.
the mechanisms of resistance to antimicrobials by biofilm cells are still largely unclear and require further research.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the biofilm mode of growth is a stress for bacteria and the biofilm is a hostile place.
there are multiple mechanisms of biocide resistance in biofilms, and that the resistance is not simply the sum of the resistance of the individual planktonic cells.
biofilm formation is the major cause of the failure of antimicrobial therapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
biofilm-growth per se is not sufficient for the development of a resistance phenotype.
biofilms are not just a passive accumulation of cells.
biofilms are heterogeneous and that multiple factors contribute to the development of resistance.
